title: Field deployment runbook: initialize, scale, and rotation playbook
open_issues: Certificate rotation automation not integrated with KMS in airgapped sites
Terraform state refresh sometimes times out on low-bandwidth VPNs
Need health-check thresholds documented for autoscaler tunables
content:
Purpose
This is a practical field runbook for initial bootstrapping, planned scaling, and node rotations for the Private Control Plane (VPC or on-prem). It is intentionally pragmatic: commands, quick checks, known gotchas, and rollback recipes. Use for customer onboards and ops during maintenance windows.

Audience and assumptions
- Audience: SREs, private-deploy engineers, solutions engineers on customer cutover days.
- Assumes remote access to customer jump host or VPN and access to their KMS/LDAP where required.
- Assumes Terraform-aware operator with aws/azure/gcloud CLIs installed and a copy of the infra repo.
- Cluster flavor: K8s-based control plane nodes with dedicated DB (managed or self-hosted).

Preflight checklist (run before any changes)
- Confirm maintenance window and customer contact (phone + Slack)
- Confirm backups: control-plane DB snapshot completed and stored offsite (s3/gcs)
- Confirm remote state is readable: terraform state pull --state=remote
- Verify SSH access to all provisioner jump hosts and control-plane nodes
- Confirm KMS keys are accessible from operator environment (test decrypt/encrypt)
- Ensure monitoring alerts are muted for planned maintenance if appropriate
- Confirm current software versions: terraform providers, module versions, k8s server version

Bootstrap / initial setup quick sequence (minimal path)
1) Networking and DNS
   - Validate VPC subnets and routing match template. Check route tables and NAT gateways.
   - Validate DNS zones: control-plane.*, api.internal -> point to LB IPs. Test: dig @<customer-dns> control-plane.example.internal A

2) Secrets & KMS
   - Ensure KMS key exists and operator IAM can encrypt/decrypt. Test: aws kms encrypt/decrypt or gcloud kms encrypt/decrypt.
   - Upload initial TLS certs to the secret store used by the control plane (Vault/K8s secrets)

3) Remote state & Terraform modules
   - Clone infra repo and checkout tag referenced in onboarding doc.
   - Important module note: pin module redwood/controlplane-module to v1.7.x for initial deploy. Do NOT use v2.x during onboarding unless compatibility sign-off.
   - Run: terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=<remote-state>\"
   - Run: terraform plan -var-file=env/customer.tfvars and inspect diffs carefully for unexpected recreate operations

4) Provision control-plane instances (first pass)
   - Apply with conservative counts: control_plane_count = 3 (for HA), bootstrap instances = 1
   - Command: terraform apply -var-file=env/customer.tfvars -target=module.controlplane.bootstrap
   - After apply, validate nodes register with k8s: kubectl get nodes --context=<cp-context>

5) Post-bootstrap validation
   - Smoke test API endpoints: curl -sk https://control-plane.example.internal/healthz
   - Check KV cache persistence and kafka/postgres connections if applicable
   - Check TLS certs and service account tokens are present

Scaling playbook (planned increases in capacity)
- When to scale: sustained CPU or memory >70% for control plane pods for 10+ minutes, or queue latency rising.
- Strategy: scale nodes in increments (20-30%) and allow 15–30 minutes for caching warmup.
- Terraform note: change control_plane_instance_type or control_plane_count in customer.tfvars, then terraform plan/apply. For rolling scale use: terraform apply -target=module.controlplane.autoscaler -var='control_plane_desired_count=6'

Scaling validation
- watch kubectl get pods -n redwood-system to see new pods get scheduled
- monitor token-per-request latency in Console (route: /api/generate latency p50/p95)
- ensure prefix cache warmup shows increased hit-rate metric after new nodes register

Node rotation / OS/kernel/security patch rotation
- Goals: rotate nodes with zero customer-visible downtime. Use rolling replacement with 1 node at a time.
- Steps: 
  1. Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m\  
  2. Verify pods rescheduled and readiness probes passed for all replicas\  
  3. SSH into node and run upgrade scripts (or trigger image bake process if immutable)\  
  4. Reboot if necessary, then kubectl uncordon <node>
  5. Wait 10–15m and run smoke tests against control-plane endpoints
- Terraform note: avoid simultaneous terraform apply and manual rotations on the same nodes. If you need to update instance templates, prefer creating new nodes and letting the old ones drain. Example pattern: increase desired_count by 1, wait for new node, drain oldest, decrease desired_count.

Upgrade plan (control plane software, Terraform modules)
- Principles: small, reversible steps. Always test in staging that mirrors customer topology.
- Module upgrade recipe:
  1. Create a branch in infra repo and update module version constraint in root module (e.g. ~> 1.8.0 -> 1.9.0).
  2. Run terraform init -upgrade and terraform plan. Inspect diffs for resource replacements.
  3. Run canary apply: apply only to 1 customer or to a single AZ via target flags.
  4. Monitor for 60–90 minutes. If regressions, revert branch and apply previous state.
- Rolling deployment of control-plane binaries:
  - Deploy new binary to 1 canary node. Run integration smoke tests (auth, generate, embeddings).
  - If OK, increase canary set to 25% nodes, then 50%, then 100%.

Rollback recipes
- If Terraform plan shows destructive operations you did not expect: abort and open a rollback flag. Do not apply.
- If after apply there is a live regression: revert to previous module version and apply. For node-level regressions, drain affected nodes and either roll back image or bring new nodes with prior image.
- DB migration rollback: if migration fails, restore DB from pre-upgrade snapshot and scale down new control plane nodes to force old code (ensure compatibility).

Observability & validation checklist (post-change)
- k8s: all pods Ready and no CrashLoopBackOffs
- Metrics: API p50/p95 within 15% of baseline, token cost per request stable
- Logs: no increase in error rates > 2x baseline for 30m
- Traces: tail latency spikes investigated (Console tracing link)
- Billing: token throughput not unexpectedly high (watch Console per-token counters)

Terraform module notes and gotchas (field operator tips)
- State locking: for low-bandwidth sites increase retries and timeouts in remote state backend to avoid spurious conflicts.
- Provider upgrades: pin provider versions in providers.tf; upgrading providers usually requires minor state tweaks.
- Mutable vs immutable nodes: prefer immutable (AMI/container image) upgrades where possible. When changing instance templates, create new instance group first.
- Sensitive outputs: avoid printing decrypted secrets in plan output; set sensitive=true on outputs in modules.
- Plan review: watch for changes to aws_autoscaling_group/launch_template resources which often trigger full replacement

Commands & quick references
- terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=<state-bucket>\"
- terraform plan -var-file=env/customer.tfvars -out=plan.out
- terraform apply "plan.out"
- kubectl get pods -n redwood-system --context=<cp-context>
- kubectl drain node-7 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
- curl -sS -k https://control-plane.example.internal/healthz | jq .status

Notes to self / field fragments (informal)
- If jump host has flaky NAT, run terraform from cloud CI runner and apply via remote-exec to control path.
- For airgapped installs, pre-stage all provider plugins and images on local registry; test terraform init in an isolated environment first.
- We saw a case where kube-proxy metrics caused high FD usage after rotation; increase node ulimit if kernel upgrade introduced change.

Postmortem checklist (if something goes wrong)
- Capture: full terraform plan output, kube events, pod logs, system journal on nodes, database logs, and monitor snapshots
- Recreate the sequence in staging with recorded inputs
- File JIRA with root cause, mitigation, and followup action (e.g., module hardening, additional checks)

Appendix: quick TF variable mapping
- control_plane_count: number of control-plane instances
- control_plane_instance_type: instance size or machine type
- enable_node_autorepair: toggles cloud provider health checks and replacement
- kms_key_id: KMS key used for secrets

Appendix: common on-site phone script (for customer ops)
- \"Hi — we are starting the maintenance window now. Expected total disruption: none. If you see anything, call this number and we will pause immediately.\"

Last updated notes
- 2025-03-12: initial drafted runbook from field notes
- 2025-03-20: added terraform module pin guidance and canary steps after staging test
